# Knowledge in the vernacular; translation movements (`vernacular_translation`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/communication.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Communication & information (`communication`)
- Deps: helped by printing_press, alphabet_writing, universal_schooling
- Core idea: Write learned and practical knowledge (medicine, law, mathematics, technique, scripture) in the language people speak, and translate key works into it. Anyone who can read their mother tongue can then learn, check and argue, instead of only those trained in Latin, classical Chinese or Sanskrit. Large organised translation programmes, with patrons paying teams of bilingual scholars to render whole libraries, move a civilisation's knowledge into another. Technical terms must be coined and kept consistent, and one dialect chosen as the written standard.
- Pitfalls:
  - Ignoring the danger: translating scripture could be heresy (Tyndale was executed in 1536)
  - Forgetting what the learned language gave: an audience across all of Europe or East Asia; scholars kept writing Latin for that reason
  - Translating without fixed technical terms: every translator invents his own and the texts cannot be compared
  - Assuming translation began with the Renaissance: the Arabic translation movement and Chinese Buddhist translations are earlier and larger
- History: china: 2nd–7th c. – Buddhist scriptures translated from Indian languages in large state-sponsored bureaus (Kumarajiva c. 400, Xuanzang 7th c.); 1917 movement for writing in vernacular Chinese (baihua); india: 5th c. BC onwards – the Buddha teaches in vernacular Prakrit rather than Sanskrit; 12th–17th c. devotional poets write in regional languages (Tulsidas' Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, 1570s); islamic: 8th–10th c. – the Graeco-Arabic translation movement in Baghdad renders Greek, Syriac, Persian and Sanskrit science and philosophy into Arabic (Hunayn ibn Ishaq); east_asia: 1446 – Hangul promulgated so that common people can write; Korean translations of Buddhist and Confucian texts follow; europe: 12th c. – Toledo translations from Arabic into Latin; c. 1304 Dante defends the vernacular; 1380s Wycliffite Bible; 1522–1534 Luther's German Bible; 1632 Galileo's Dialogue in Italian; 1637 Descartes' Discourse in French
- Read:
  - Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998)
  - Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (2006)
  - Peter Burke, Languages and Communities in Early Modern Europe (2004)
